Netflix has no shortage of shows that arrive with a huge premise, dominate the conversation for a few weeks, and then disappear into the streaming abyss. The best four-season shows, however, have managed to become something far more lasting. They've built worlds worth returning to, introduced characters who feel like old friends (or spectacularly bad influences), and delivered enough story to feel substantial without becoming an endless commitment.

From chaotic coming-of-age comedies to bleak crime dramas, these series prove that some of Netflix's best original shows are also among its most rewatchable. Sure, they may have very different tones and ambitions, but they all share one important quality: they know just how to keep you coming back for more, especially with their succinct number of seasons.

8
'Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt' (2015–2019)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/unbreakable-kimmy-schmidt-ellie-kemper-jane-krakowski-titus-burgess.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Ellie Kemper as Kimmy Schmidt, Jane Krakowski as Jacqueline White, and Tituss Burgess as Titus Andromedon in 'Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt.'

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

After spending 15 years in an underground bunker, Kimmy Schmidt (Ellie Kemper) is rescued from the doomsday cult that kidnapped her and moves to New York City to start a new life. Armed with an infectious optimism and absolutely no idea how the modern world works, Kimmy takes a job as a nanny, makes new friends, and attempts to experience all the things she missed while growing up in captivity.

Compared to other comedies, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt shines for its commitment to the ridiculous. Kimmy's fish-out-of-water perspective turns ordinary New York life into a series of bizarre discoveries, while supporting players like the fabulous Titus (Tituss Burgess) and Jacqueline (Jane Krakowski) give the show an endless supply of comedic chaos. Better still, beneath the vibrancy and surreal jokes lies a surprisingly warm story about rebuilding one's life. Think of it as wonderfully silly television with a big heart.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/atypical-season-4-Keir-Gilchrist-trailer-social.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Netflix

Sam Gardner (Keir Gilchrist) is an 18-year-old on the autism spectrum who decides he is ready to start dating. Along the way, his search for a girlfriend sets off a chain reaction in his family, as his parents and younger sister begin confronting their own changing relationships and expectations.

Atypical is at its best when it lets its characters be funny, complicated, and occasionally a little bit wrong. Gilchrist brings a wonderfully understated charm to Sam, while other members of the family are given plenty of personality. Atypical is a forgotten Netflix series with a knack for finding humor in everyday awkwardness, but it also makes room for genuinely touching moments about growing up and learning to let people change.

'Never Have I Ever' (2020–2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/never-have-i-ever.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Matreyi Ramakrishnan and Poorna Jaggarnnathan in Never Have I Ever

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

After the sudden death of her father, Devi Vishwakumar (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) is determined to make her sophomore year of high school her best one yet by becoming popular, getting good grades, and finally finding a boyfriend. Sadly, her plans are complicated by her grief, her complex relationship with her mother, and the fact that she is spectacularly bad at making sensible decisions.

Never Have I Ever is easily one of Netflix's most entertaining coming-of-age comedies, as they completely understand how funny, embarrassing, and occasionally painful adolescence can be. Ramakrishnan gives Devi a wonderfully messy energy, whether it's because she's experiencing drama in her romantic life or just typical teenage hijinks. Better still, the show is anchored by a genuine emotional center, particularly in its exploration of life's most heartbreaking moments.

5
'The Umbrella Academy' (2019–2024)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F68a4112c5ceac-IMG_1589%20copy.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/the-umbrella-academy-season-2-cast-image.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Netflix

After the mysterious death of their adoptive father, seven estranged siblings with extraordinary abilities reunite at the Umbrella Academy. But as they attempt to uncover the truth about his death, they discover that the world is on the brink of apocalypse, forcing them to put aside their disorderly family dynamics and work together to save it.

From the minute the show appeared on the streaming network, The Umbrella Academy made a name for itself as the new, dysfunctional, semi-superhero show. The Hargreeves siblings are a wonderfully chaotic ensemble, with each character bringing a different kind of energy to the story. Sure, it can be messy—especially with the show's combination of time travel, bizarre mysteries, and eccentric villains—but that's often part of its charm.

4
'Sex Education' (2019–2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/sex-education-poster-season-1-netflix.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Netflix

When awkward teenager Otis Milburn (Asa Butterfield) begins giving relationship advice to his classmates, he discovers that his knowledge of sex and relationships is far more useful than he expected. Seeing a lucrative opportunity, Otis, his best friend Eric (Ncuti Gatwa), and the ambitious Maeve (Emma Mackey) open an unofficial sex-therapy clinic on campus where Otis can help his peers navigate everything from first love to sexual insecurity.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9

Sex Education stood out among the coming-of-age genre as it brilliantly balanced its outrageous humor with genuine affection for its characters and themes. A true ensemble piece, filled with memorable personalities, the show had a knack for making even the most awkward teenage situations feel both hilarious and surprisingly relatable. Its willingness to talk openly about sex and identity was extremely refreshing, all while its emotional moments gave the comedy a true sense of weight. Even when it gets a little too ambitious, Sex Education remains wonderfully significant in how it explores what it means to truly grow up.

3
'Castlevania' (2017–2021)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/sypha-alucard-and-trevor-in-castlevania-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Sypha, Alucard and Trevor walking side by side in Castlevania

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

When his human wife is executed by the people of Wallachia, Dracula (Graham McTavish) declares war on humanity and unleashes an army of monsters upon the country. The only people standing in his way are Trevor Belmont (Richard Armitage), the last surviving member of a disgraced monster-hunting family, powerful magician Sypha Belnades (Alejandra Reynoso), and Alucard (James Callis), Dracula's half-human son. Together, they must work together to stop Dracula's campaign of revenge before it destroys the world.

Combining brutal action with a surprisingly rich emotional tale, Castlevania has become one of the most impressive adult animated shows of the last few years. The artwork is gorgeous, the fight scenes are spectacular, and the characters are far more complicated than the usual heroes and villains set up. The core trio has fantastic chemistry, while Dracula's grief gives the story a tragic center that makes the violence feel more than just spectacle. It's dark, stylish, and occasionally very funny, with a world that feels completely and fully realized.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/the-sinner-bill-pullman-jessica-biel.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Bill Pullman as Harry Ambrose walks behind a handcuffed Jessica Biel as Cora in The Sinner Season 1.

blocks.x: Image via USA Network

With every season following a different crime, Harry Ambrose (Bill Pullman) investigates what initially appears to be a straightforward case before uncovering the complicated history behind it. And rather than simply asking who committed the crime, the show focuses more on why someone would do something so terrible, gradually revealing the secrets, trauma, and psychological pressures that led to the violence.

What makes The Sinner so compelling is its ability to turn a familiar crime-story formula into something much more psychologically unsettling. Pullman gives Ambrose a wonderfully flawed, introspective presence, while the changing cases allow the show to explore a range of disturbing and often unexpected human motivations. It's not always an easy watch, but it's constantly atmospheric and intriguing, resulting in a truly underrated crime anthology that feels less interested in tidy answers than in the uncomfortable questions that remain.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Ozark-Finale.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Jason Bateman and Laura Linney in the 'Ozark' finale

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

When a money laundering deal goes terribly wrong, financial adviser Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman) is forced to move his family from Chicago to the Ozarks. There, he must find a way to launder millions of dollars for a Mexican cartel to save their lives. Meanwhile, his wife, Wendy (Laura Linney), becomes increasingly involved in the criminal world, leading their decisions to draw them deeper into a dangerous web of corruption.

Ozark is easily one of Netflix's most gripping crime dramas simply because it knows how to make even the smallest decision spiral into the most catastrophic of consequences. Bateman and Linney are both formidable forces, with their performances giving the Byrdes a complicated dynamic that makes their relationship as fascinating as the criminal plot itself. The show is dark, tense, and often genuinely unsettling. But it also has a strangely sharp sense of humor that keeps it from becoming relentlessly bleak (as would other tales of ambition and survival).

'Sex Education' (2019–2023)

Image via Netflix

When awkward teenager Otis Milburn (Asa Butterfield) begins giving relationship advice to his classmates, he discovers that his knowledge of sex and relationships is far more useful than he expected. Seeing a lucrative opportunity, Otis, his best friend Eric (Ncuti Gatwa), and the ambitious Maeve (Emma Mackey) open an unofficial sex-therapy clinic on campus where Otis can help his peers navigate everything from first love to sexual insecurity.

Sex Education stood out among the coming-of-age genre as it brilliantly balanced its outrageous humor with genuine affection for its characters and themes. A true ensemble piece, filled with memorable personalities, the show had a knack for making even the most awkward teenage situations feel both hilarious and surprisingly relatable. Its willingness to talk openly about sex and identity was extremely refreshing, all while its emotional moments gave the comedy a true sense of weight. Even when it gets a little too ambitious, Sex Education remains wonderfully significant in how it explores what it means to truly grow up.

'Castlevania' (2017–2021)

Image via Netflix

When his human wife is executed by the people of Wallachia, Dracula (Graham McTavish) declares war on humanity and unleashes an army of monsters upon the country. The only people standing in his way are Trevor Belmont (Richard Armitage), the last surviving member of a disgraced monster-hunting family, powerful magician Sypha Belnades (Alejandra Reynoso), and Alucard (James Callis), Dracula's half-human son. Together, they must work together to stop Dracula's campaign of revenge before it destroys the world.

Combining brutal action with a surprisingly rich emotional tale, Castlevania has become one of the most impressive adult animated shows of the last few years. The artwork is gorgeous, the fight scenes are spectacular, and the characters are far more complicated than the usual heroes and villains set up. The core trio has fantastic chemistry, while Dracula's grief gives the story a tragic center that makes the violence feel more than just spectacle. It's dark, stylish, and occasionally very funny, with a world that feels completely and fully realized.

'The Sinner' (2017–2021)

Image via USA Network

With every season following a different crime, Harry Ambrose (Bill Pullman) investigates what initially appears to be a straightforward case before uncovering the complicated history behind it. And rather than simply asking who committed the crime, the show focuses more on why someone would do something so terrible, gradually revealing the secrets, trauma, and psychological pressures that led to the violence.

What makes The Sinner so compelling is its ability to turn a familiar crime-story formula into something much more psychologically unsettling. Pullman gives Ambrose a wonderfully flawed, introspective presence, while the changing cases allow the show to explore a range of disturbing and often unexpected human motivations. It's not always an easy watch, but it's constantly atmospheric and intriguing, resulting in a truly underrated crime anthology that feels less interested in tidy answers than in the uncomfortable questions that remain.

'Ozark' (2017–2022)

Image via Netflix

When a money laundering deal goes terribly wrong, financial adviser Marty Byrde (Jason Bateman) is forced to move his family from Chicago to the Ozarks. There, he must find a way to launder millions of dollars for a Mexican cartel to save their lives. Meanwhile, his wife, Wendy (Laura Linney), becomes increasingly involved in the criminal world, leading their decisions to draw them deeper into a dangerous web of corruption.

Ozark is easily one of Netflix's most gripping crime dramas simply because it knows how to make even the smallest decision spiral into the most catastrophic of consequences. Bateman and Linney are both formidable forces, with their performances giving the Byrdes a complicated dynamic that makes their relationship as fascinating as the criminal plot itself. The show is dark, tense, and often genuinely unsettling. But it also has a strangely sharp sense of humor that keeps it from becoming relentlessly bleak (as would other tales of ambition and survival).
